lessons.title: Let’s count the real space locations first, and then talk about band representation
lessons.summary: Use orbit–stabilizer to distinguish site induction from full-k-star induction.

sections.title: One seed generates a complete orbit
sections.text: Apply every Seitz representative to seed r₀, then remove duplicates modulo full lattice translations. A general position in space group 2 generates r₀ and −r₀; an inversion center generates one site. These are real-space sites in a primitive cell, not arms of a momentum star.

sections.title: stabilizer To really fix the site
sections.text: If Rr₀+t differs from r₀ by an integer lattice vector L, replace the representative’s translation with t−L to obtain a site-stabilizer element that fixes r₀ exactly. Output lists both the subtracted L and the actual fixing translation.

sections.title: The local degree of freedom determines the fiber dimension
sections.text: Put an s orbital at each site for m-dimensional Bloch fiber; put a complete p triplet for 3m dimensions. p is reducible at some sites stabilizer , so it cannot be directly called an irreducible local representation, nor can it be automatically called EBR.

sections.title: Check between classroom and workbench
sections.text: First look at the site table and stabilizer table, and then observe the decomposition of Γ point character . The two-dimensional representation of group 2 general position s is divided into one part even parity and one part odd parity. Local D numbers are sorted with calculations and the inversion character is applied to identify them.

lessons.title: How to add phase to the sites crossing the primitive cell boundary
lessons.summary: Derive lattice-translation remainders, actions between fibers, and screw squares from periodic Bloch sums.

sections.title: Fix the gauge first
sections.text: Use the periodic gauge: Bloch coefficients include lattice vector T but omit orbital center rₐ from the exponential. Translation T_L therefore has eigenphase exp(−2πi k·L). Gauge changes alter matrix elements, so formulas from different gauges must not be mixed.

sections.title: Two parts of one operation
sections.text: After solving Rrₐ+t=r_b+L, the matrix block is the local s/p transformation multiplied by exp[−2πi(R⁻ᵀk)·L]. A general operation maps the k fiber to R⁻ᵀk. Only little-group operations preserving k modulo reciprocal-lattice vectors have physical characters within the same fiber.

sections.title: A screw operation squares to a translation
sections.text: This site’s space group 4 has its screw axis along z. Applying 2₁ twice gives a z-directed lattice translation, so its representation squares to −I at k_z=1/2 and has eigenvalues ±i. Omitting phases when sites cross cell boundaries incorrectly gives the square +I.
sections.formula: U_S(k)² = exp(−2πi k_z) I； λ_{±} = ±exp(−iπ k_z)

sections.title: View branch exchange along axis
sections.text: The second plot shows real and imaginary parts of complex eigenvalues, not band energies. The positive and negative labels exchange when k_z increases by one reciprocal period. Energy degeneracy, connectivity and insulating behavior additionally require a Hamiltonian and other constraints; this curve alone cannot establish them.

lessons.title: From matrices to characters and little-group decomposition
lessons.summary: Examining phase, dimensionality and irreducible decomposition with the boundary of group 19 projective representation .

sections.title: Retain lattice-translation remainders in Seitz multiplication
sections.text: The product of two selected representatives is not necessarily equal to the third representative in the catalog, and may be an additional full cell translation Δ. At fixed k this difference becomes a factor system and ordinary multiplication of quotient group cannot be imposed on the Bloch matrix.

sections.title: orthogonal inner product to multiplicity
sections.text: does the inner product with the verified little group irreducible character of the same factor system. The output must satisfy both the nonnegative integer multiplicity , the original character reconstruction, and the conservation of total dimensionality; simply listing some representation names is not enough to constitute a decomposition.

sections.title: Why are four s orbitals not equal to four one-dimensional representations?
sections.text: A general orbit of space group 19 has four sites. Screw phases at R=(1/2,1/2,1/2) give nontrivial projective multiplication, producing two copies of the same two-dimensional little-group irrep. This dimension comes from spatial operations and translation phases, rather than a Kramers conclusion imposed by spin time reversal.

sections.title: Local results and global problems
sections.text: Switching to point Γ, the factor system is trivial, and the s four-dimensional fiber is divided into four one-dimensional terms. D1 with different k is not the same global label. If you want to further connect energy bands, please enter the compatibility relationship class; this module does not automatically provide full-region connectivity diagrams or topological classifications.

lessons.title: The difference between perovskite sites and orbital centers
lessons.summary: Compares the induced space of the cubic origin, body-centered and three face-centered sites.

sections.title: Separate structural sites and electron filling
sections.text: The 1a, 1b and 3c positions of Pm−3m are site prototypes. The three face-center sites of 3c often illustrate the oxygen sublattice of ideal cubic perovskites, but this experiment places abstract local orbitals only, without charge transfer, covalent hybridization, actual oxygen levels or occupancies.

sections.title: p orbitals at the origin form a polar-vector triplet
sections.text: At Γ, local pₓ,pᵧ,p_z form the three-dimensional polar-vector representation of O_h, commonly labeled T_{1u}. Its inversion matrix is −I₃ and character −3. The program still supplies only verified local D labels, without identifying them as standard database labels.

sections.title: orbit center influence boundary character
sections.text: Local inversion is even for s orbitals at both the origin and body center. However, after inversion the body-center seed must be shifted by (−1,−1,−1) to return to the same  primitive cell  site, so parity changes sign at some boundary points. Orbital centers and the Bloch gauge must therefore be retained.
sections.formula: χ_I(k;r₀) = exp(+4πi k·r₀) (s orbital, inversion center)

sections.title: cross-module project
sections.text: Record the dimensions and inversion characters of 1a-s, 1b-s, and 3c-p at Γ, X, and R. Then discuss local orbitals in the crystal-field classroom and connectivity in the band-compatibility classroom. These address different levels of the same structural problem; these sampled data alone cannot determine whether the complete material is topological.

exercises.title: Group 2: turn the site count into the fiber dimension
exercises.prompt: Choose the general-position two-site orbit and an s orbital, then work through the Γ-point derivation by hand.

steps.prompt: Is the inversion image of a general-position site r₀ equivalent to the site itself?
steps.hint: r₀=(0.17,0.23,0.31); check whether 2r₀ is an integer vector.
choices: Not equivalent; the orbit has two sites
Yes; the orbit contains only one point
Determined by the k point
steps.explanation: 2r₀ is not an integer vector, so r₀ and −r₀ are two sites within the primitive cell.

steps.prompt: What is the order of the seed site's stabilizer?
steps.hint: quotient group  has order 2; use the orbit– stabilizer  relation.

steps.prompt: What is the trace of the inversion matrix for the two s orbitals at Γ?
steps.hint: Inversion exchanges the two points, so the matrix diagonal receives no fixed-point contributions.
steps.explanation: The site-permutation matrix is off-diagonal: the inversion character is 0 and the identity character is 2.

steps.prompt: What are the multiplicities of the two one-dimensional parity representations?
choices: One even and one odd
Two even, zero odd
Zero even states, two odd states
steps.explanation: Adding and subtracting gives n_g=n_u=1; the dimensions also balance.

exercises.title: Group 4: derive ±i from two sites
exercises.prompt: Select the  screw axis  boundary preset and derive the result along the program's BC z axis.

steps.prompt: What spatial operation results from applying a 2₁ screw twice?
steps.hint: Two half-lattice translations combine into one full translation, and a twofold rotation squares to the identity.
choices: Translate half a lattice spacing along z
Translation by one lattice period along z
The identity, with no translation
steps.explanation: S²={E|0,0,1}; squaring only the point operation instead of the complete space-group operation loses the translation.

steps.prompt: At k_z=1/2 in the periodic Bloch gauge, what is the phase of a full lattice translation?
Which pair gives the spinless screw eigenvalues?
choices: +i and −i
+1 and −1
Two +i eigenvalues
steps.explanation: Two-site s orbitals provide the branches ±i;  time reversal  is not imposed here.

steps.prompt: Does the branch exchange of λ_{+} and λ_{−} in the figure give the band energy of the material?
steps.hint: There are no Hamiltonian parameters for this experiment.
choices: It has been proven that the insulating and topological
No; they are symmetry eigenvalues only
The conduction band and valence band have been given
steps.explanation: Symmetry representations constrain energy models but are not themselves energy dispersions or complete topological classifications.

exercises.title: Group 19: Two copies of the two-dimensional projective little group representation
exercises.prompt: Use the R-point s-orbital preset and check each basis for the decomposition.

steps.prompt: A general site orbit has four points, each carrying one s orbital. What is the fiber dimension?
steps.hint: The dimensionality is the number of sites multiplied by the number of local orbitals.
steps.explanation: m=4, d=1, so fiber dimension 4; no additional spin multiplication.

steps.prompt: Can point R ignore the extra integer vector when the representative elements are multiplied?
steps.hint: The component of k is 1/2, and some integer translations contribute a negative sign.
choices: No, it will change the factor system
Yes; full lattice translations always have phase 1
Only not available when there is SOC
steps.explanation: Bloch translation characters can be −1 at the boundary, quotient group needs to use the corresponding projective representation .

steps.prompt: The table of values ​​shows that only one 2D class irreducible representation contributes, what is its multiplicity ?
steps.explanation: The two two-dimensional representations give exactly four-dimensional induced space; character inner product and reconstruction can be independently verified.

steps.prompt: Can this two-dimensionality be directly called spin Kramers degeneracy?
steps.hint: This module does not contain spin and time reversal .
choices: Yes, the two-dimensional must be equal to Kramers
Only group 19 is called Kramers
No, what is verified here is the space little group projective algebra
steps.explanation: Kramers pairing requires an appropriate antiunitary symmetry squaring to −1; this experiment constructs only ordinary-space-group Bloch actions.

exercises.title: Place p orbitals on three face-centered sites
exercises.prompt: Start with the 3c-p prototype, then compare it with p orbitals at the origin.

steps.prompt: What is the orbit multiplicity m of 3c?
steps.hint: The site table contains three coordinate permutations.
steps.explanation: The three face-centered sites form one orbit with m=3.

steps.prompt: What is the fiber dimension given by the complete p triplet at each point?
steps.hint: 3 orbitals per point, but no spin.
steps.explanation: is 3×3=9; 18 requires additional spin, which is not available here.

steps.prompt: What is the character of the origin p triplet under inversion?
steps.hint: Every component of a polar vector changes sign.
steps.explanation: The inversion matrix is ​​−I₃, and the trace is −3. Don't think of it as axial vector .

steps.prompt: Has the full nine-dimensional 3c-p space been established as one EBR?
steps.hint: First determine whether the local representation is irreducible and check the complete EBR criterion.
choices: No, the program only verifies the decomposition of induced representation and little group
Yes; every site orbit is an EBR
Yes, as long as the dimensions are odd
steps.explanation: p is reducible in the 3c position stabilizer , and this module does not implement general elementary determination or full Brillouin zone topological analysis.

cases.title: Orbital center and boundary parity
cases.summary: Compare the inversion character of the origin s and the body center s at point X for the same local dual symmetry.
cases.assumption: Abstract spin-free local orbit; fixed period specification and the same origin, topological conclusions cannot be directly given from two sampling points.

cases.title: Along-axis tangent in three-dimensional spiral crystal
cases.summary: tracks the spiral eigenphase on the z-tangential line of SG4/19, connecting the real-space half-lattice displacement and the momentum space factor system.
cases.assumption: This is an instructional model of the three-dimensional space group acting on a k-line, with no actual materials or hopping Hamiltonian specified.

cases.title: Site skeleton of ideal cubic perovskite
cases.summary: Use 1a/1b/3c of Pm−3m to understand the different sublattices and calculate a nine-dimensional representation of p orbitals at three face-centered sites.
cases.assumption: Only borrows the perovskite-type site skeleton; does not predict the true electronic bands, filling, phonon , or phase transitions of SrTiO₃ or BaTiO₃.

cases.title: Boundary of group 19 representation dimension
cases.summary: Compare the local representations of Γ and R, and then use the existing compatibility relationship to discuss in class why cross-k tracking cannot only recognize the D number.
cases.assumption: No inverse unitary symmetry is attached; the two-dimensionality of space projective representation and the spin Kramers mechanism must be distinguished.
